entities.name: Titanic
entities.fact: The Titanic struck an iceberg and sank in the North Atlantic on its maiden voyage in April 1912; its wreck lies about 3,800 metres down.

entities.name: Lusitania
entities.fact: The Cunard liner Lusitania was torpedoed by a German submarine off the south coast of Ireland in May 1915 and sank in about 18 minutes.

entities.name: Bismarck
entities.fact: The German battleship Bismarck was sunk by the Royal Navy in the North Atlantic in May 1941, three days after it had destroyed HMS Hood.

entities.name: USS Arizona
entities.fact: The battleship USS Arizona exploded and sank during the attack on Pearl Harbor in December 1941, and its wreck still leaks oil today.

entities.name: Costa Concordia
entities.fact: The cruise ship Costa Concordia struck rocks and capsized off the Italian island of Giglio in January 2012; it was refloated two years later and scrapped.

entities.name: Endurance
entities.fact: Shackleton's ship Endurance was crushed by pack ice and sank in the Weddell Sea in 1915; its remarkably preserved wreck was found in 2022 at about 3,000 metres.

entities.name: Mary Rose
entities.fact: Henry VIII's warship Mary Rose sank in the Solent in 1545 and was raised in 1982; its hull is now displayed in Portsmouth.

entities.name: Vasa
entities.fact: The Swedish warship Vasa sank on its maiden voyage in 1628, minutes after leaving Stockholm, and was raised almost intact in 1961.

entities.name: Britannic
entities.fact: Titanic's sister ship Britannic, serving as a hospital ship, struck a mine and sank in the Aegean Sea in 1916.

entities.name: Andrea Doria
entities.fact: The Italian liner Andrea Doria sank off Nantucket in 1956 after colliding in fog with the Swedish ship Stockholm.

entities.name: HMS Hood
entities.fact: The battlecruiser HMS Hood blew up and sank within minutes after being hit by Bismarck in 1941; only three of her crew survived.

entities.name: Yamato
entities.fact: Yamato, one of the two largest battleships ever built, was sunk by American aircraft in April 1945 on a one-way mission to Okinawa.

entities.name: USS Indianapolis
entities.fact: USS Indianapolis was torpedoed in July 1945 after delivering atomic-bomb parts, and many of the survivors in the water were taken by sharks before rescue came.

entities.name: Kursk
entities.fact: The Russian submarine Kursk sank in the Barents Sea in August 2000 after torpedo explosions, with the loss of all 118 aboard.

entities.name: USS Maine
entities.fact: USS Maine exploded and sank in Havana harbour in 1898, helping to spark the Spanish-American War.

entities.name: HMS Erebus
entities.fact: HMS Erebus, one of the ships of Franklin's lost Arctic expedition, sank in the Canadian Arctic and was found in shallow water in 2014.

entities.name: HMS Terror
entities.fact: HMS Terror, Franklin's second ship, was found almost intact in 2016 in Terror Bay, off King William Island in the Canadian Arctic.

entities.name: Admiral Graf Spee
entities.fact: The German pocket battleship Admiral Graf Spee was scuttled by its own crew off Montevideo in December 1939 after the Battle of the River Plate.

entities.name: Rainbow Warrior
entities.fact: The Greenpeace ship Rainbow Warrior was sunk by bombs planted by French agents in Auckland harbour in 1985.

entities.name: Sewol
entities.fact: The South Korean ferry Sewol capsized and sank in April 2014 with the loss of more than 300 people, most of them schoolchildren.

entities.name: General Belgrano
entities.fact: The Argentine cruiser General Belgrano was torpedoed by a British submarine and sank during the Falklands War in 1982.

entities.name: USS Monitor
entities.fact: The Civil War ironclad USS Monitor sank in a storm off Cape Hatteras on the last day of 1862; its turret was raised in 2002.

entities.name: Bounty
entities.fact: After the famous mutiny, the Bounty was burned and sunk by the mutineers at Pitcairn Island in 1790.

entities.name: Carpathia
entities.fact: Carpathia, the ship that rescued Titanic's survivors, was itself torpedoed and sunk in the Atlantic in 1918.

entities.name: Estonia
entities.fact: The ferry Estonia sank in the Baltic Sea in September 1994 after its bow door failed, killing 852 people.

entities.name: Queen Anne's Revenge
entities.fact: Blackbeard's flagship Queen Anne's Revenge ran aground and was lost off Beaufort, North Carolina, in 1718; its wreck was found in 1996.

entities.name: Wilhelm Gustloff
entities.fact: The German liner Wilhelm Gustloff was torpedoed in the Baltic in January 1945; with roughly 9,000 dead, it is the deadliest sinking in history.

entities.name: Doña Paz
entities.fact: The Philippine ferry Doña Paz collided with a tanker and sank in December 1987, the deadliest peacetime shipwreck ever, with more than 4,000 dead.

entities.name: Batavia
entities.fact: The Dutch East India Company ship Batavia was wrecked on a reef off Western Australia in 1629, and a bloody mutiny followed among the survivors.

entities.name: Nuestra Señora de Atocha
entities.fact: The Spanish treasure galleon Nuestra Señora de Atocha sank in a hurricane off the Florida Keys in 1622; its gold and silver were found in 1985.

entities.name: Whydah Gally
entities.fact: The pirate ship Whydah Gally sank in a storm off Cape Cod in 1717; its wreck, found in 1984, was the first authenticated pirate shipwreck.

entities.name: H. L. Hunley
entities.fact: The Confederate submarine H. L. Hunley sank in 1864 shortly after becoming the first submarine to sink an enemy warship.

entities.name: Lancastria
entities.fact: The troopship Lancastria was bombed and sunk off Saint-Nazaire in June 1940, Britain's worst ever maritime disaster.

entities.name: San José
entities.fact: The Spanish galleon San José was sunk by British warships off Cartagena, Colombia, in 1708, carrying a treasure now valued in the billions.

entities.name: SS Central America
entities.fact: The steamer SS Central America, the 'Ship of Gold', sank in a hurricane off the Carolinas in 1857 with tonnes of California gold aboard.

entities.name: Essex
entities.fact: The whaleship Essex was rammed and sunk by a sperm whale in the Pacific in 1820, inspiring Herman Melville's Moby-Dick.

entities.name: New York
entities.fact: New York Harbour is one of the great natural harbours of the world and was the main gateway for immigrants arriving in the United States.

entities.name: Lisbon
entities.fact: Lisbon sits where the Tagus meets the Atlantic, and Vasco da Gama sailed from here in 1497 on the first voyage from Europe to India.

entities.name: Miami
entities.fact: The Port of Miami on Biscayne Bay calls itself the cruise capital of the world and handles more cruise passengers than any other port.

entities.name: Boston
entities.fact: Boston's harbour on the Atlantic was the scene of the Boston Tea Party in 1773, when colonists dumped tea into the water in protest at British taxes.

entities.name: Rio de Janeiro
entities.fact: Rio de Janeiro means 'River of January', the name given by Portuguese sailors who reached Guanabara Bay in January 1502.

entities.name: Halifax
entities.fact: Halifax, Nova Scotia, has one of the largest natural harbours in the world, and many of the Titanic's victims are buried in the city's cemeteries.

entities.name: Reykjavik
entities.fact: Reykjavik, the world's northernmost national capital, grew up around its harbour and Iceland's fishing fleet.

entities.name: Casablanca
entities.fact: Casablanca is Morocco's biggest city and its main Atlantic port, famous around the world thanks to the 1942 film.

entities.name: Cape Town
entities.fact: Cape Town's harbour on Table Bay faces the Atlantic, where the cold Benguela Current keeps the sea far chillier than on the Indian Ocean side of the Cape.

entities.name: Buenos Aires
entities.fact: Buenos Aires sits on the Río de la Plata estuary, which opens into the Atlantic, and its name means 'fair winds'.

entities.name: Lagos
entities.fact: Lagos, Nigeria's largest city, grew around a lagoon opening onto the Atlantic, and its name is Portuguese for 'lakes'.

entities.name: Dakar
entities.fact: Dakar, on the Cap-Vert peninsula, is the westernmost city on the African mainland and a major Atlantic port.

entities.name: Porto
entities.fact: Porto, at the mouth of the Douro river, gave its name both to Portugal and to port wine.

entities.name: Charleston
entities.fact: Charleston's harbour, where the Ashley and Cooper rivers meet the Atlantic, saw the first shots of the American Civil War at Fort Sumter in 1861.

entities.name: Havana
entities.fact: Havana's sheltered harbour on the Straits of Florida was the gathering point for Spain's treasure fleets before they crossed the Atlantic.

entities.name: Nassau
entities.fact: Nassau, capital of the Bahamas, was a notorious pirate haven in the early 1700s, home to Blackbeard and Charles Vane.

entities.name: San Juan
entities.fact: San Juan, Puerto Rico, is guarded by El Morro, a Spanish fortress begun in 1539 to protect the harbour entrance.

entities.name: Montevideo
entities.fact: Montevideo, Uruguay's capital and main port, lies on the Río de la Plata near where the Graf Spee was scuttled in 1939.

entities.name: Cádiz
entities.fact: Cádiz, on a narrow spit into the Atlantic, was founded by the Phoenicians and is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in western Europe.

entities.name: Vigo
entities.fact: Vigo, in Galicia, is Europe's biggest fishing port, landing fish from fleets that work the Atlantic as far away as the Falklands.

entities.name: Bilbao
entities.fact: Bilbao's port on the Bay of Biscay is one of Spain's busiest, and the city was reinvented by the Guggenheim museum in 1997.

entities.name: Brest
entities.fact: Brest, on the far western tip of Brittany, is one of France's two main naval bases, with a huge natural harbour opening onto the Atlantic.

entities.name: Cork
entities.fact: Cork harbour is one of the largest natural harbours in the world, and Cobh at its mouth was the Titanic's last port of call.

entities.name: Norfolk
entities.fact: Norfolk, Virginia, at the mouth of Chesapeake Bay, is home to the largest naval base in the world.

entities.name: Las Palmas
entities.fact: Las Palmas de Gran Canaria is a major Atlantic port where Columbus's ships stopped for repairs in 1492 before crossing to the Americas.

entities.name: Luanda
entities.fact: Luanda, Angola's capital, is a major Atlantic port whose bay is sheltered by the long sand island of Ilha de Luanda.

entities.name: St. John's
entities.fact: St. John's, Newfoundland, is the easternmost city in North America and one of the oldest English settlements on the continent.

entities.name: Salvador
entities.fact: Salvador, Brazil's first capital, sits on the Bay of All Saints, one of the largest bays on the Atlantic coast of South America.

entities.name: Walvis Bay
entities.fact: Walvis Bay, Namibia's main port, takes its name from the whales that once gathered in its waters; it means 'whale bay'.

entities.name: Abidjan
entities.fact: Abidjan, Ivory Coast's economic capital, became a major Atlantic port in the early 1950s when the Vridi Canal was cut through to its lagoon.

entities.name: Freetown
entities.fact: Freetown, Sierra Leone, was founded in 1792 as a home for freed slaves and has one of the largest natural harbours in the world.

entities.name: Santos
entities.fact: Santos, near São Paulo, is the busiest port in Latin America and the main gateway for Brazil's coffee exports.

entities.name: Mar del Plata
entities.fact: Mar del Plata is Argentina's main seaside resort and its biggest fishing port.

entities.name: Ponta Delgada
entities.fact: Ponta Delgada, the largest city of the Azores, sits on the island of São Miguel in the middle of the North Atlantic.

entities.name: Nuuk
entities.fact: Nuuk, Greenland's capital, lies on the Labrador Sea and is one of the smallest capital cities in the world.

entities.name: A Coruña
entities.fact: A Coruña's Tower of Hercules is the oldest Roman lighthouse still in use, guiding ships on Spain's Atlantic coast.

entities.name: New Bedford
entities.fact: New Bedford, Massachusetts, was the whaling capital of the world in the 1800s and is today the highest-value fishing port in the United States.

entities.name: Trawler
entities.fact: A trawler catches fish by dragging a large net, the trawl, through the water or along the seabed behind it.

entities.name: Canoe
entities.fact: Polynesian voyagers crossed thousands of kilometres of open Pacific in double-hulled sailing canoes, settling islands as far apart as Hawaii and New Zealand.

entities.name: Kayak
entities.fact: The kayak was developed by Inuit and other Arctic peoples as a sealed one-person hunting boat for seals and other sea animals.

entities.name: Yacht
entities.fact: The word yacht comes from the Dutch 'jacht', meaning hunt, from the fast, light ships once used to chase pirates.

entities.name: Sailboat
entities.fact: Sailboats are driven by the wind alone, and the oldest known picture of a sail, on an Egyptian pot, is more than 5,000 years old.

entities.name: Schooner
entities.fact: A schooner is a sailing ship with two or more masts whose main sails run fore-and-aft, a rig that made it a favourite of fishermen and smugglers.

entities.name: Galleon
entities.fact: Galleons were the big, multi-decked sailing ships that carried Spain's silver across the Atlantic in the 16th and 17th centuries.

entities.name: Longship
entities.fact: Viking longships were long, narrow and shallow-draughted, able to cross open sea and yet be rowed up shallow rivers to raid inland.

entities.name: Catamaran
entities.fact: A catamaran has two parallel hulls joined by a frame, a design borrowed from the fishing craft of southern India; the name comes from the Tamil for 'tied wood'.

entities.name: Container ship
entities.fact: The biggest container ships are about 400 metres long and can carry more than 20,000 standard shipping containers.

entities.name: Ferry
entities.fact: Ferries carry passengers and vehicles on regular routes across the water, and some of the busiest in the world cross the English Channel and the Baltic.

entities.name: Submarine
entities.fact: Nuclear submarines can stay underwater for months at a time, limited only by the food they carry for the crew.

entities.name: Tugboat
entities.fact: Tugboats are small but extremely powerful, built to push and pull ships many times their own size in and out of harbours.

entities.name: Dinghy
entities.fact: A dinghy is a small open boat, often carried aboard or towed behind a larger vessel as a tender to reach the shore.

entities.name: Clipper ship
entities.fact: Clipper ships were the fast sailing ships of the mid-1800s, built for speed on the tea and wool runs; Cutty Sark is the most famous survivor.

entities.name: Oil tanker
entities.fact: The largest oil tankers ever built, the ultra-large crude carriers, could carry more than 500,000 tonnes of oil in a single voyage.

entities.name: Cruise ship
entities.fact: The largest cruise ships today carry more than 5,000 passengers and are longer than three football pitches laid end to end.

entities.name: Dhow
entities.fact: Dhows are the traditional lateen-rigged sailing vessels of the Arabian Sea and Indian Ocean, used for centuries in trade between Arabia, East Africa and India.

entities.name: Junk
entities.fact: The Chinese junk, with its battened sails, was sailing the seas centuries before similar rigs appeared in Europe, and Zheng He's treasure fleet used giant junks.

entities.name: Caravel
entities.fact: The caravel was the small, nimble Portuguese ship of the 1400s used by explorers along the African coast; Columbus's Niña and Pinta were caravels.

entities.name: Sloop
entities.fact: A sloop is a sailing boat with a single mast and one headsail, the most common rig on modern yachts.

entities.name: Dory
entities.fact: The dory is a flat-bottomed, high-sided rowing boat once launched from fishing schooners on the Grand Banks to set cod lines.

entities.name: Outrigger canoe
entities.fact: An outrigger canoe has a float lashed alongside the hull for stability, and such canoes carried Austronesian peoples across the Pacific and Indian Oceans.

entities.name: Purse seiner
entities.fact: A purse seiner surrounds a school of fish with a long wall of net, then draws the bottom closed like a purse; most tuna and sardines are caught this way.

entities.name: Trireme
entities.fact: The trireme was the ancient Greek warship rowed by three banks of oarsmen, which won the Battle of Salamis in 480 BC.

entities.name: Galley
entities.fact: Galleys were oar-driven warships that dominated the Mediterranean from ancient times until the Battle of Lepanto in 1571.

entities.name: Crab boat
entities.fact: Crab boats work the Bering Sea in winter, hauling heavy steel pots in freezing seas, a job made famous by the television series Deadliest Catch.

entities.name: Coracle
entities.fact: A coracle is a small, round boat of woven wood covered in hide or canvas, still used by a few fishermen in Wales and India.

entities.name: Currach
entities.fact: The currach is an Irish boat of tarred canvas or hide stretched over a wooden frame, used for fishing in the Atlantic off the west coast.

entities.name: Sampan
entities.fact: The sampan is a flat-bottomed wooden boat of China and Southeast Asia, used for fishing and as a floating home in harbours and rivers.

entities.name: Felucca
entities.fact: The felucca is a traditional wooden sailing boat with one or two lateen sails, used on the Nile and along the Red Sea and Mediterranean coasts.

entities.name: Carrack
entities.fact: The carrack was the big, round-hulled ocean ship of the 1400s and 1500s; Columbus's Santa María and Magellan's Victoria were carracks.

entities.name: Cog
entities.fact: The cog was the sturdy single-masted cargo ship of the medieval Hanseatic League, trading across the North Sea and the Baltic.

entities.name: Fishing smack
entities.fact: A fishing smack was a sailing boat, often with a wet well to keep the catch alive, used around the British coast into the 20th century.

entities.name: Longliner
entities.fact: A longliner fishes with a main line that can stretch for tens of kilometres, hung with thousands of baited hooks.

entities.name: Umiak
entities.fact: The umiak is a large open skin boat of the Inuit, rowed or paddled by several people and used for hunting whales and moving families along the coast.

entities.name: Knarr
entities.fact: The knarr was the broad Viking cargo ship that carried settlers and livestock across the open North Atlantic to Iceland, Greenland and Vinland.

entities.name: Kelp
entities.fact: Kelps are large brown seaweeds that form underwater forests along cold, rocky coasts, anchored by a root-like holdfast rather than true roots.

entities.name: Nori
entities.fact: Nori is dried, pressed sheets of the red seaweed laver, grown on nets in shallow Japanese bays and used to wrap sushi rolls.

entities.name: Seagrass
entities.fact: Seagrasses are true flowering plants, not seaweeds, with roots and underwater flowers, and their meadows store carbon far faster than forests on land.

entities.name: Wakame
entities.fact: Wakame is the brown seaweed in miso soup and seaweed salad; outside Asia it is an invasive species that spread on the hulls of ships.

entities.name: Kombu
entities.fact: Kombu is dried kelp, the seaweed that gives Japanese dashi stock its savoury umami taste; monosodium glutamate was first isolated from it in 1908.

entities.name: Sargassum
entities.fact: Sargassum is a floating brown seaweed held up by gas-filled bladders; huge rafts of it give the Sargasso Sea its name and shelter young sea turtles.

entities.name: Giant kelp
entities.fact: Giant kelp is the largest seaweed, growing up to about 45 metres long and as much as half a metre in a single day.

entities.name: Bladderwrack
entities.fact: Bladderwrack is the brown seaweed with paired air bladders along its fronds, common on rocky shores and the original source of iodine.

entities.name: Sea lettuce
entities.fact: Sea lettuce is a bright green seaweed with fronds only two cells thick, which can bloom into 'green tides' where sewage or farm runoff enriches the water.

entities.name: Dulse
entities.fact: Dulse is a red seaweed eaten for centuries in Ireland, Scotland and Iceland, often dried and sold as a salty snack.

entities.name: Irish moss
entities.fact: Irish moss, or carrageen, is a small red seaweed whose extract carrageenan thickens ice cream, toothpaste and plant milks.

entities.name: Eelgrass
entities.fact: Eelgrass is a seagrass of cool northern coasts whose meadows are nurseries for young cod, herring and crabs.

entities.name: Mangrove
entities.fact: Mangroves are trees that grow in salt water along tropical shores, with tangled stilt roots that trap mud and shelter young fish.

entities.name: Bull kelp
entities.fact: Bull kelp grows a single long stem topped by a gas-filled float the size of a grapefruit, and can reach more than 30 metres in a single season.

entities.name: Turtle grass
entities.fact: Turtle grass is the dominant seagrass of the Caribbean, grazed by green turtles and manatees.

entities.name: Sugar kelp
entities.fact: Sugar kelp has a long, crinkled single blade and gets its name from the sweet white powder, mannitol, that forms on it when dried.

entities.name: Oarweed
entities.fact: Oarweed is a common European kelp with a thick stem and a blade split into fingers, exposed only at the lowest tides.

entities.name: Hijiki
entities.fact: Hijiki is a brown seaweed eaten in Japan, usually dried and black; it is known for holding unusually high levels of arsenic.

entities.name: Sea grapes
entities.fact: Sea grapes are a green seaweed with tiny bubble-like beads that pop in the mouth, eaten fresh in Okinawa and the Philippines.

entities.name: Caulerpa taxifolia
entities.fact: Caulerpa taxifolia, the 'killer alga', escaped from an aquarium into the Mediterranean in the 1980s and smothered thousands of hectares of seabed.

entities.name: Dead man's fingers
entities.fact: Dead man's fingers is a dark green, spongy, finger-shaped seaweed that is really a single giant cell with many nuclei.

entities.name: Red mangrove
entities.fact: The red mangrove stands on arching prop roots and drops long, pencil-shaped seedlings that float away to take root on other shores.

entities.name: Knotted wrack
entities.fact: Knotted wrack, or egg wrack, is a long-lived brown seaweed with single egg-shaped air bladders along its fronds, harvested for alginate and fertiliser.

entities.name: Coralline algae
entities.fact: Coralline algae are red seaweeds that lay down hard limestone skeletons, cementing coral reefs together like pink mortar.

entities.name: Gutweed
entities.fact: Gutweed is a bright green, tube-shaped seaweed of upper shores and estuaries, named for its hollow, gut-like fronds.

entities.name: Sea palm
entities.fact: The sea palm looks like a tiny palm tree and lives only on the most wave-battered rocks of the Pacific coast of North America.

entities.name: Maerl
entities.fact: Maerl is a free-living coralline seaweed that grows into gravel-like nodules, forming seabed beds that take centuries to build up.

entities.name: Halimeda
entities.fact: Halimeda is a green seaweed built from chalky segments; its dead flakes make up much of the white sand on tropical beaches.

entities.name: Peacock's tail
entities.fact: Peacock's tail is a small fan-shaped brown seaweed of warm rock pools, banded with white lime and shimmering blue-green.

entities.name: Thongweed
entities.fact: Thongweed, or sea spaghetti, grows from a small button into straps up to about 2 metres long and is sold fresh as a sea vegetable.

entities.name: Serrated wrack
entities.fact: Serrated wrack is the toothed-edged brown seaweed of the lower shore, with no air bladders, sheltering many small animals beneath it.

entities.name: Channelled wrack
entities.fact: Channelled wrack lives at the very top of the shore, where it can dry out for days between tides and still revive.

entities.name: Winged kelp
entities.fact: Winged kelp, or alaria, has a long blade with a midrib and is farmed in the North Atlantic and eaten as 'Atlantic wakame'.

entities.name: Neptune's necklace
entities.fact: Neptune's necklace is a seaweed of strings of water-filled beads, common on rocky shores of Australia and New Zealand.

entities.name: Southern bull kelp
entities.fact: Southern bull kelp has a honeycomb-like inner flesh that keeps it afloat, and Māori once used its blades as bags to store food.

entities.name: Neptune grass
entities.fact: Neptune grass, Posidonia oceanica, forms vast Mediterranean meadows; one clone off Ibiza is thought to be up to about 100,000 years old.

entities.name: Sea urchin
entities.fact: Sea urchins graze kelp with a five-toothed jaw called Aristotle's lantern, and their creamy orange roe, uni, is a sushi-bar delicacy.

entities.name: Green turtle
entities.fact: Adult green sea turtles graze on seagrass and algae, which stains their fat green and gives them their name; they may live for 70 years or more.

entities.name: Manatee
entities.fact: Manatees are slow plant eaters that graze on seagrass for several hours a day and can live for 60 years or more; Snooty, a Florida manatee, lived to 69.

entities.name: Parrotfish
entities.fact: Parrotfish scrape algae from rock and dead coral with beak-like teeth, grinding up the rock and excreting it as fine white sand.

entities.name: Dugong
entities.fact: The dugong is the only fully marine mammal that lives almost entirely on seagrass, leaving tell-tale furrows through the meadows, and it can live for 70 years.

entities.name: Marine iguana
entities.fact: The marine iguana of the Galápagos is the only lizard that feeds in the sea, diving to graze algae from the rocks and sneezing out the salt afterwards.

entities.name: Abalone
entities.fact: Abalone are large sea snails that graze on kelp; served raw as awabi in sushi bars, they are now mostly farmed in tanks because wild stocks have crashed.

entities.name: Limpet
entities.fact: Limpets graze algae from rocks with a tongue-like radula whose teeth are among the strongest biological materials known, and each returns to its own home scar.

entities.name: Common periwinkle
entities.fact: The common periwinkle is a shore snail that grazes on seaweed and algae; carried from Europe to North America, it is now abundant there too.

entities.name: Surgeonfish
entities.fact: Surgeonfish, or tangs, are reef grazers that crop algae all day and carry a scalpel-like blade on each side of the tail.

entities.name: Sea hare
entities.fact: Sea hares are soft-bodied sea slugs that eat seaweed, and the colour of their defensive ink depends on the colour of the seaweed they have eaten.

entities.name: Kelp crab
entities.fact: The kelp crab lives in kelp forests of the Pacific coast of North America, where it feeds mostly on the kelp itself.

entities.name: Conch
entities.fact: The queen conch of the Caribbean grazes on algae and seagrass detritus with a long snout, and its pink-lipped shell is prized.

entities.name: Rabbitfish
entities.fact: Rabbitfish are shy reef grazers with venomous fin spines that feed on seaweed; they are named for their blunt, rabbit-like faces.

entities.name: Purple sea urchin
entities.fact: Purple sea urchins have stripped vast stretches of California's kelp forests since 2014, leaving 'urchin barrens' of bare rock.

entities.name: Damselfish
entities.fact: Many damselfish farm their own gardens of algae on the reef, fiercely chasing away any fish, diver or turtle that comes to graze.

entities.name: Red sea urchin
entities.fact: The red sea urchin feeds on kelp off the Pacific coast of North America and can live for more than 100 years.

entities.name: Chiton
entities.fact: Chitons are eight-plated molluscs that creep over rocks at night, scraping algae with a radula tipped with magnetite, a hard iron mineral.

entities.name: Opaleye
entities.fact: The opaleye is a Californian kelp-forest fish with bright blue-green eyes that feeds mainly on seaweed.

entities.name: Sea chub
entities.fact: Sea chubs, or rudderfish, are unusual among reef fish in eating mostly brown seaweeds such as sargassum, and they often follow boats.

entities.name: Pinfish
entities.fact: The pinfish of the western Atlantic eats more and more seagrass as it grows, and is a common bait fish in Florida.

entities.name: Black turban snail
entities.fact: Black turban snails crowd the rocky shores of California, grazing on seaweed and drift kelp.

entities.name: Unicornfish
entities.fact: Unicornfish are large surgeonfish with a horn on the forehead that graze on brown seaweeds on Indo-Pacific reefs.

entities.name: Long-spined sea urchin
entities.fact: The long-spined sea urchin keeps Caribbean reefs clear of seaweed; after a disease killed most of them in 1983, algae overgrew many reefs.

entities.name: Top shell
entities.fact: Top shells are cone-shaped grazing snails of rocky shores that scrape seaweed and algal film from the rocks.

entities.name: Sand hopper
entities.fact: Sand hoppers are tiny shrimp-like crustaceans that live in and feed on rotting seaweed washed up along the strandline.

entities.name: Lawnmower blenny
entities.fact: The lawnmower blenny is named for its habit of cropping algae, which makes it a popular cleaner for reef aquariums.

entities.name: Lettuce sea slug
entities.fact: The lettuce sea slug eats green algae and keeps their chloroplasts alive inside its frilly body, where they go on making sugar from sunlight.

entities.name: Eastern emerald elysia
entities.fact: The eastern emerald elysia steals chloroplasts from the alga it eats and can then live for months on photosynthesis alone, like a leaf that crawls.

entities.name: Kelp fly
entities.fact: Kelp flies lay their eggs in rotting seaweed on the strandline, and their larvae feed on it, becoming food for shore birds.

entities.name: Wigeon
entities.fact: The wigeon is a dabbling duck that grazes on eelgrass in estuaries in winter, often alongside brant geese.

entities.name: Kina
entities.fact: Kina is New Zealand's native sea urchin, a kelp grazer whose roe is a traditional Māori delicacy.

entities.name: Green sea urchin
entities.fact: The green sea urchin grazes kelp in cold northern waters and is fished for its roe in Maine and Norway.

entities.name: Halfbeak
entities.fact: Halfbeaks are slender surface fish with a long lower jaw; many species feed on seagrass and floating algae.

entities.name: Brant goose
entities.fact: The brant is a small sea goose that depends on eelgrass; when disease wiped out eelgrass on both sides of the Atlantic in the 1930s, brant numbers crashed.

entities.name: Tuna
entities.fact: Tunas are warm-blooded, torpedo-shaped sprinters among the fastest fish in the sea; in Japan tuna is maguro, the most popular sushi fish of all.

entities.name: Salmon
entities.fact: Raw salmon only became a sushi fish in the 1980s, when Norway began marketing its farmed Atlantic salmon to Japan; wild Pacific salmon are still caught by the million.

entities.name: Shrimp
entities.fact: Shrimp are the most valuable seafood traded worldwide; more than half of those eaten now come from farms, and sushi shrimp (ebi) are usually boiled and butterflied.

entities.name: Eel
entities.fact: Freshwater eel, unagi, is never served raw because its blood is toxic; for sushi it is grilled and glazed with a sweet soy sauce.

entities.name: Crab
entities.fact: Crab appears in sushi as kani, but much of the 'crab' in California rolls is kamaboko, a paste made from Alaska pollock.

entities.name: Yellowtail
entities.fact: Yellowtail, or hamachi, is a fast-swimming Japanese amberjack farmed in large numbers in Japan and served raw for its buttery flesh.

entities.name: Pufferfish
entities.fact: Pufferfish, fugu, carry a poison with no antidote in their organs, so only licensed chefs in Japan may prepare them as sashimi.

entities.name: Octopus
entities.fact: Octopus, tako, is usually boiled before it is sliced for sushi, which turns its skin purple-red and gives the tentacles their chewy bite.

entities.name: Squid
entities.fact: Squid, ika, is served raw in sushi bars as a translucent white slice, often scored to make it tender.

entities.name: Scallop
entities.fact: Scallops swim by clapping their shells, and the big muscle that does the clapping is the part eaten; Japan and China farm them by the million on hanging ropes.

entities.name: Mackerel
entities.fact: Mackerels are fast, striped schooling fish with tiny finlets before the tail; they spoil quickly, so for sushi (saba) they are cured in salt and vinegar.

entities.name: Flounder
entities.fact: Flounders are flatfish that start life with an eye on each side; one eye migrates across the head as they grow, and they lie camouflaged on the seabed.

entities.name: Sardine
entities.fact: Sardines are small oily schooling fish, tinned by the million and also served raw as iwashi in Japanese sushi bars in summer.

entities.name: Anchovy
entities.fact: Anchovies are small, strongly flavoured fish salted and tinned for pizzas, Caesar dressing and Worcestershire sauce.

entities.name: Herring
entities.fact: Herring is eaten pickled in Scandinavia, raw with onions in the Netherlands and smoked as kippers in Britain; it once supported Europe's biggest fisheries.

entities.name: Halibut
entities.fact: Halibut are the largest flatfish, reaching over 2 metres and 200 kilograms, and their firm white flesh makes them a prized food fish.

entities.name: Trout
entities.fact: Trout are freshwater relatives of salmon; the rainbow trout is farmed worldwide and is one of the most commonly eaten freshwater fish.

entities.name: Snapper
entities.fact: Snappers are warm-water reef fish prized for their firm white flesh; the red snapper of the Gulf of Mexico is the most famous, and many other fish are sold under its name.

entities.name: Catfish
entities.fact: Catfish are whiskered bottom-dwellers; the channel catfish is the most farmed fish in the United States, and Vietnamese basa fills supermarket freezers worldwide.

entities.name: Grouper
entities.fact: Groupers are big-mouthed reef predators that swallow prey whole with a sudden gulp; they are a staple of Caribbean and Southeast Asian restaurants.

entities.name: Carp
entities.fact: Common carp has been farmed for food for more than 2,000 years and is still the traditional Christmas Eve dish in Poland and the Czech Republic.

entities.name: Hake
entities.fact: Hake is a slim relative of cod and the favourite fish of Spain, which eats more of it than any other country.

entities.name: Oyster
entities.fact: Oysters have been farmed since Roman times, and today almost all the oysters eaten are grown on racks, ropes or bags in sheltered bays.

entities.name: Mussel
entities.fact: Mussels are farmed on ropes hung from rafts and longlines, needing no feed at all because they filter plankton from the sea.

entities.name: Clam
entities.fact: Clams are farmed by sowing tiny hatchery-raised seed clams onto tidal flats and harvesting them a few years later.

entities.name: Sturgeon
entities.fact: Sturgeons are armoured, shark-tailed fish older than the dinosaurs that can live for over 100 years; they are farmed for caviar now that wild Caspian stocks are protected.

entities.name: Bonito
entities.fact: Bonitos are striped, tuna-like fish of the mackerel family; in Japan 'bonito' usually means the skipjack, seared as katsuo tataki or dried into bonito flakes.

entities.name: Bluefin tuna
entities.fact: The Atlantic bluefin tuna can weigh more than 600 kilograms and is warm-blooded, keeping its muscles warmer than the sea so it can sprint after prey.

entities.name: Pacific bluefin tuna
entities.fact: The Pacific bluefin tuna is the species behind Tokyo's record new-year auctions; one sold for about 333 million yen in 2019.

entities.name: Southern bluefin tuna
entities.fact: The southern bluefin tuna was fished down to a small fraction of its original numbers and is now ranched in sea pens off South Australia.

entities.name: Yellowfin tuna
entities.fact: Yellowfin tuna, sold as ahi, is a fast, warm-water tuna with long yellow fins that is the common tuna in poke and sushi outside Japan.

entities.name: Albacore
entities.fact: Albacore, the 'white tuna' of canned tuna, has the longest pectoral fins of any tuna and is served as shiro maguro in sushi bars.

entities.name: Skipjack tuna
entities.fact: Skipjack is the most-caught tuna in the world and the one in most tins; in Japan it is katsuo, dried into bonito flakes and seared as tataki.

entities.name: Bigeye tuna
entities.fact: The bigeye tuna, with large eyes for hunting in dim deep water, is a major catch for longline fleets and is sold as sashimi-grade ahi in Hawaii.

entities.name: Blackfin tuna
entities.fact: The blackfin tuna is the smallest of the true tunas, rarely over a metre long, and is found only in the western Atlantic.

entities.name: Longtail tuna
entities.fact: The longtail tuna is a coastal tuna of the Indo-Pacific that stays in shallow seas rather than roaming the open ocean.

entities.name: Dogtooth tuna
entities.fact: The dogtooth tuna is a reef-hunting member of the tuna family with large, conical teeth; it is a bonito rather than a true tuna.

entities.name: Kawakawa
entities.fact: The kawakawa, or mackerel tuna, is a small coastal tuna of the Indo-Pacific with wavy stripes on its back and dark spots under its pectoral fins.

entities.name: Little tunny
entities.fact: The little tunny, or false albacore, is the most common tuna in the Atlantic, a small, fast, scribble-patterned fish loved by fly anglers but rarely eaten.

entities.name: Frigate tuna
entities.fact: The frigate tuna is a small, torpedo-shaped tuna found worldwide in warm seas, important both as food and as bait.

entities.name: Bullet tuna
entities.fact: The bullet tuna is one of the smallest members of the tuna family, found worldwide in warm seas and rarely more than 50 centimetres long.

entities.name: Slender tuna
entities.fact: The slender tuna is a Southern Ocean member of the tuna family that feeds on krill and is rarely seen by anyone but longline crews.

entities.name: Atlantic bonito
entities.fact: The Atlantic bonito is a fast, striped, tuna-like schooling fish of the Atlantic and Mediterranean, eaten salted or grilled in Turkey as palamut.

entities.name: Eastern Pacific bonito
entities.fact: The eastern Pacific bonito ranges from Chile to Alaska and is a common catch for anglers off California.

entities.name: Striped bonito
entities.fact: The striped bonito of the Indo-Pacific is eaten as sashimi in Japan, where it is called hagatsuo.

entities.name: Plain bonito
entities.fact: The plain bonito is an unstriped, deep-bodied bonito of the eastern Atlantic and Mediterranean.

entities.name: Wahoo
entities.fact: The wahoo is a long, razor-toothed member of the mackerel family and one of the fastest fish in the sea; Hawaiians call it ono, meaning delicious.

entities.name: King mackerel
entities.fact: The king mackerel, or kingfish, is a big, fast Spanish mackerel of the western Atlantic, chased by anglers off Florida and known to leap clear of the water.

entities.name: Spanish mackerel
entities.fact: The Atlantic Spanish mackerel is a spotted, fast-swimming schooling fish of the US east coast and Gulf of Mexico, popular with anglers and on the plate.

entities.name: Cero
entities.fact: The cero is a Spanish mackerel of the Caribbean with a row of yellow-orange streaks and spots along its sides.

entities.name: Narrow-barred Spanish mackerel
entities.fact: The narrow-barred Spanish mackerel is a big, fast Indo-Pacific fish with wavy bars on its flanks, a prize of Australian and Gulf fishing.

entities.name: Japanese Spanish mackerel
entities.fact: The Japanese Spanish mackerel, sawara, is a spring fish in Japan, grilled with miso or served as lightly seared sashimi.

entities.name: Atlantic mackerel
entities.fact: The Atlantic mackerel is caught in huge numbers in the North Atlantic; it has no swim bladder, so it must keep swimming to stay afloat.

entities.name: Chub mackerel
entities.fact: The chub mackerel is one of the world's biggest fish catches, taken in huge numbers off Japan, Chile and Peru, and is the saba of Japanese sushi bars.

entities.name: Indian mackerel
entities.fact: The Indian mackerel is the everyday fish of South and Southeast Asia, caught in huge numbers and fried, curried or dried.

entities.name: Blue mackerel
entities.fact: The blue mackerel, or slimy mackerel, is a spotted mackerel of Australian and New Zealand waters, mostly used as bait and for canning.

entities.name: Butterfly kingfish
entities.fact: The butterfly kingfish is the oddest member of the tuna family, a cold-water Southern Ocean fish with big scales and a heater organ that warms its brain and eyes.

entities.name: Olive flounder
entities.fact: The olive flounder, hirame, is Japan's premier sashimi flatfish, farmed widely in Japan and Korea; its fin muscle, engawa, is a chewy delicacy.

entities.name: Tiger puffer
entities.fact: The tiger puffer, torafugu, is the most prized fugu; its liver and ovaries hold a deadly poison, so only licensed chefs in Japan may prepare it as sashimi.

entities.name: Swordfish
entities.fact: Swordfish slash at squid with a flat bill and are among the fastest fish in the sea; their meaty steaks are eaten worldwide and served raw as mekajiki in Japan.

entities.name: Red sea bream
entities.fact: Red sea bream, tai, is Japan's celebration fish, served as sashimi at weddings and New Year because its name sounds like 'medetai', meaning happy.

entities.name: Japanese sea bass
entities.fact: Japanese sea bass, suzuki, is a summer sashimi fish that changes its name as it grows, a 'success fish' in Japanese tradition.

entities.name: Japanese horse mackerel
entities.fact: Horse mackerel, aji, is one of the most common fish in Tokyo sushi bars, served raw with grated ginger and spring onion.

entities.name: Conger eel
entities.fact: Conger eel, anago, is a saltwater eel simmered until soft and served with a sweet sauce in sushi; it is leaner than freshwater unagi.

entities.name: Flying fish
entities.fact: Flying fish sprint to about 60 kilometres per hour to burst from the water, then glide up to 200 metres on wing-like fins; their roe is tobiko in sushi.

entities.name: Cuttlefish
entities.fact: Cuttlefish, sumi-ika, is served raw in sushi bars, where its thick, sweet white flesh is prized over squid in winter.

entities.name: Northern shrimp
entities.fact: The northern prawn is served raw as amaebi, 'sweet shrimp', often with its fried head on the side.

entities.name: King crab
entities.fact: Red king crab legs, taraba-gani, are served in sushi; the crab is caught in the cold Bering Sea and off Hokkaido.

entities.name: Snow crab
entities.fact: Snow crab, zuwai-gani, is a long-legged cold-water crab whose sweet leg meat appears in sushi and crab rolls.

entities.name: Surf clam
entities.fact: The surf clam, hokkigai, is served in sushi with its tip blanched, which turns the foot a bright red.

entities.name: Geoduck
entities.fact: The geoduck is a huge Pacific clam with a siphon up to a metre long; it can live for more than 150 years, is farmed in Washington State and is sliced thin for sushi as mirugai.

entities.name: Mantis shrimp
entities.fact: The mantis shrimp, shako, is boiled and served over rice in Edo-style sushi; it is a fierce predator with club-like or spear-like claws.

entities.name: Monkfish
entities.fact: Monkfish, the angler of the seabed with a huge mouth, has firm tail meat nicknamed 'poor man's lobster', and its liver is served in sushi as ankimo.

entities.name: Greater amberjack
entities.fact: The greater amberjack, kanpachi in Japan, is a fast, powerful hunter of the open water, farmed in sea pens and served as firm, mild sashimi.

entities.name: Pacific saury
entities.fact: Pacific saury, sanma, is caught by the hundreds of thousands of tonnes in the northwest Pacific and is an autumn favourite grilled whole in Japan.

entities.name: Gizzard shad
entities.fact: The gizzard shad, kohada, is the fish by which Tokyo sushi chefs are judged; it is salted and pickled in vinegar before serving.

entities.name: Cod
entities.fact: Atlantic cod built the economies of Newfoundland and New England and is the classic fish of British fish and chips; its stocks collapsed off Canada in 1992.

entities.name: Tilapia
entities.fact: Tilapia is a freshwater fish farmed in warm ponds worldwide and is now one of the most eaten fish on earth; it was raised in ancient Egypt.

entities.name: Mahi-mahi
entities.fact: Mahi-mahi, or dorado, is a fast-growing, brilliantly coloured open-ocean fish that is among the fastest swimmers in the sea and a popular restaurant catch.

entities.name: Haddock
entities.fact: Haddock, with a black 'thumbprint' behind the gill, is the favourite fish-and-chips fish in Scotland and northern England and is smoked as finnan haddie.

entities.name: European sea bass
entities.fact: The European sea bass, sold as branzino in restaurants, is heavily farmed in the Mediterranean and is one of Europe's favourite white fish.

entities.name: Alaska pollock
entities.fact: Alaska pollock is the most-caught fish in the United States and the fish inside most fish fingers, fast-food fish sandwiches and surimi crab sticks.

entities.name: Common sole
entities.fact: The Dover sole is the classic flatfish of French and English cooking, named for the port that supplied London's restaurants.

entities.name: Barramundi
entities.fact: Barramundi, the Asian sea bass, is farmed widely in Australia and Southeast Asia; it starts life as a male and later changes into a female.

entities.name: Plaice
entities.fact: Plaice, with its orange spots, is the most important flatfish of European fisheries and a fish-and-chips favourite.

entities.name: Turbot
entities.fact: Turbot is a large, diamond-shaped flatfish so prized that a special pan was made for poaching it whole; today most turbot are farmed in Spain and China.

entities.name: Gilthead bream
entities.fact: The gilt-head bream, with a gold bar between its eyes, is one of the Mediterranean's most popular eating fish and is heavily farmed as orata or dorade.

entities.name: John Dory
entities.fact: John Dory has a dark spot on each flank said to be St Peter's thumbprint, and its sweet white fillets are prized by chefs.

entities.name: Walleye
entities.fact: Walleye is the most popular eating fish of the Great Lakes region and the state fish of Minnesota.

entities.name: Orange roughy
entities.fact: Orange roughy is a deep-sea fish that can live for more than 150 years, so it was fished out quickly after it became a restaurant favourite in the 1980s.

entities.name: Patagonian toothfish
entities.fact: The Patagonian toothfish was renamed 'Chilean sea bass' in 1977 to make it sell in American restaurants, where it became a hit.

entities.name: Sablefish
entities.fact: Sablefish, sold as black cod, is a buttery deep-water fish of the North Pacific, famous miso-marinated, and it can live for more than 90 years.

entities.name: Pangasius
entities.fact: Pangasius, sold as basa or river cobbler, is a Vietnamese Mekong catfish farmed in vast numbers and exported as cheap white fillets.

entities.name: Rohu
entities.fact: Rohu is a carp of South Asian rivers, the most popular eating fish in Bangladesh and eastern India.

entities.name: Milkfish
entities.fact: Milkfish is the national fish of the Philippines, farmed in coastal ponds for centuries and eaten despite its many fine bones.

entities.name: Peruvian anchoveta
entities.fact: The Peruvian anchoveta is the most heavily fished species on Earth, with catches that have topped 10 million tonnes a year, nearly all ground into fishmeal.

entities.name: Capelin
entities.fact: Capelin are small Arctic smelt caught by the hundreds of thousands of tonnes off Iceland and Norway, mostly for fishmeal and roe.

entities.name: Menhaden
entities.fact: Menhaden are oily herring relatives caught in enormous numbers along the US coast, almost all of it 'reduced' into fish oil and meal rather than eaten.

entities.name: Pink salmon
entities.fact: The pink salmon is the smallest and most abundant Pacific salmon, caught by the hundreds of millions in Alaska and Russia, mostly for canning.

entities.name: Blue whiting
entities.fact: Blue whiting is a small cod relative of the North Atlantic caught by the million tonnes for fishmeal and surimi.

entities.name: Chilean jack mackerel
entities.fact: The Chilean jack mackerel supported one of the largest fisheries in the world in the 1990s, with catches of about 5 million tonnes, before the stock crashed.

entities.name: Sand eel
entities.fact: Sand eels are not eels but slim, burrowing fish caught by Danish trawlers by the hundreds of thousands of tonnes for fishmeal, and a vital food for puffins.

entities.name: Pacific cod
entities.fact: The Pacific cod is a major fishery of the Bering Sea and Gulf of Alaska, with catches of several hundred thousand tonnes a year.

entities.name: Saithe
entities.fact: Saithe, or coley, is a dark-fleshed cousin of cod caught in huge numbers in the North Atlantic; cheaper than cod, it is often used in fish pies.

entities.name: Sprat
entities.fact: Sprats are tiny herring relatives caught by the hundreds of thousands of tonnes, smoked whole in Baltic countries and tinned as 'brisling sardines'.

entities.name: Pacific herring
entities.fact: The Pacific herring is fished mainly for its roe, sold to Japan as kazunoko, and its eggs laid on kelp are a traditional food of the Pacific Northwest.

entities.name: Norway pout
entities.fact: The Norway pout is a small cod relative of the North Sea caught almost entirely for fishmeal and oil.

entities.name: Indian oil sardine
entities.fact: The Indian oil sardine is the most important fish of India's west coast, caught by the hundreds of thousands of tonnes in the monsoon season.

entities.name: Bombay duck
entities.fact: Bombay duck is not a duck but a lizardfish caught in huge numbers off western India, where it is dried on racks and fried.

entities.name: Hoki
entities.fact: Hoki is a deep-water cod relative of New Zealand's biggest fishery, and ends up in fish fingers and fast-food fish sandwiches.

entities.name: Round sardinella
entities.fact: The round sardinella is a small schooling fish caught in huge numbers off West Africa, where it is a staple protein.

entities.name: Japanese anchovy
entities.fact: The Japanese anchovy is one of the largest catches in the northwest Pacific, eaten dried as niboshi and as tiny boiled whitebait, shirasu.

entities.name: Japanese sardine
entities.fact: The Japanese sardine catch rose above 4 million tonnes in the 1980s before collapsing, one of the most dramatic booms and busts in fishing.

entities.name: Largehead hairtail
entities.fact: The largehead hairtail is a ribbon-like, silver predator with fangs that is one of the largest fish catches in the world, mostly off China.

entities.name: Whiteleg shrimp
entities.fact: The whiteleg shrimp is the most farmed shrimp in the world, raised in coastal ponds from Ecuador to Vietnam, and is the prawn in most supermarkets.

entities.name: Pacific oyster
entities.fact: The Pacific oyster, native to Japan, is now the most farmed oyster in the world and grows on coasts from France to Australia.

entities.name: Tiger prawn
entities.fact: The black tiger prawn, with its striped shell, was the main farmed shrimp of Asia until the faster-growing whiteleg shrimp replaced it.

entities.name: Crayfish
entities.fact: The red swamp crayfish of Louisiana is now farmed by the million tonnes in China, where crayfish feasts are a summer craze.

entities.name: Japanese eel
entities.fact: The Japanese eel, unagi, cannot yet be bred commercially, so eel farms raise wild-caught glass eels in warm ponds for about a year before they are grilled as kabayaki.

entities.name: Mud crab
entities.fact: Mud crabs are farmed in mangrove ponds across Southeast Asia and sold live, tied with string, for chilli crab.

entities.name: Cobia
entities.fact: Cobia is a fast-growing open-water fish now farmed in sea cages in Vietnam, Taiwan and Panama for its firm white flesh.

entities.name: Silver carp
entities.fact: The silver carp is among the most farmed fish in the world in China, yet in American rivers it is an invader notorious for leaping out of the water at boats.

entities.name: Bighead carp
entities.fact: The bighead carp is farmed in huge quantities in China, where its large head is prized for soups.

entities.name: Sea cucumber
entities.fact: Sea cucumbers are farmed in sea ranches and ponds in China, where dried sea cucumber is a banquet luxury; the Japanese sea cucumber is the main farmed species.

entities.name: Giant river prawn
entities.fact: The giant river prawn, with its long blue claws, is farmed in freshwater ponds across Asia and sold as scampi in India.

entities.name: Red drum
entities.fact: The red drum, or redfish, is farmed in ponds and cages in Texas and China after blackened redfish made the wild fish a craze in the 1980s.

entities.name: Green-lipped mussel
entities.fact: The green-lipped mussel is farmed on ropes in New Zealand and is the country's biggest aquaculture product.

entities.name: Quahog
entities.fact: The hard clam, or quahog, is farmed along the US east coast and sold by size as littlenecks, cherrystones and chowder clams.

entities.name: Manila clam
entities.fact: The Manila clam, native to Asia, is the most farmed clam in the world and is now grown in Europe and North America too.

entities.name: Grass carp
entities.fact: The grass carp is the most farmed fish on Earth by weight, raised in Chinese ponds on grass and water plants.

entities.name: Whiting
entities.fact: Whiting is a small, soft-fleshed relative of cod that has long been a cheap staple of British chip shops.

entities.name: Ling
entities.fact: The ling is a long, slender cod relative of deep North Atlantic waters that can reach 2 metres; its salted, dried flesh is a traditional Norwegian export.

entities.name: Pollack
entities.fact: The pollack is a golden-brown European cousin of cod with a jutting lower jaw, popular with sea anglers around rocky coasts and wrecks.

entities.name: Cusk
entities.fact: The cusk, or tusk, is a single-dorsal-finned cod relative of deep North Atlantic waters, eaten in Norway and New England.

entities.name: Arctic cod
entities.fact: The Arctic cod, or polar cod, lives under the sea ice with antifreeze proteins in its blood and is the key food of seals, narwhals and seabirds.

entities.name: European hake
entities.fact: The European hake is a slim, sharp-toothed cod relative fished from Norway to West Africa; Spain eats more of it than any other country.

entities.name: Grenadier
entities.fact: Grenadiers, or rattails, are deep-sea cousins of cod with big heads and long tapering tails, among the most abundant fish on the deep seabed.

entities.name: Poor cod
entities.fact: The poor cod is a small, coppery cod relative of European coasts, too small to be worth eating but important food for larger fish.

entities.name: Pouting
entities.fact: The pouting, or bib, is a small, deep-bodied cod relative with coppery bands, common around piers and wrecks in European waters.

entities.name: Greenland cod
entities.fact: The Greenland cod is a dark, slow-growing cod of Arctic coastal waters, caught by Inuit through holes in the ice.

entities.name: Atlantic tomcod
entities.fact: The Atlantic tomcod is a small cod of North American estuaries; those in the Hudson River evolved resistance to PCB pollution in just a few decades.

entities.name: Shore rockling
entities.fact: The shore rockling is a small, eel-like cod relative with three barbels, found under stones in rock pools around Britain.

entities.name: Silver hake
entities.fact: The silver hake is the main hake of the US east coast, a fast-swimming predator of small fish that is sold there under the name whiting.

entities.name: Cape hake
entities.fact: The Cape hake is the backbone of the South African and Namibian fishing industries, caught by trawlers over the continental shelf.

entities.name: Roundnose grenadier
entities.fact: The roundnose grenadier is a deep-sea cod relative trawled at over 1,000 metres in the North Atlantic that can live for more than 50 years.

entities.name: Giant grenadier
entities.fact: The giant grenadier is a deep-water rattail of the North Pacific that grows to over 2 metres long and lives for decades.

entities.name: Navaga
entities.fact: The navaga is a small Arctic cod of the White and Barents Seas, fished through the ice in Russia in winter.

entities.name: Red cod
entities.fact: The red cod of New Zealand is a morid cod, a distant relative of the Atlantic cod, with a single chin barbel and pinkish skin.

entities.name: Greater forkbeard
entities.fact: The greater forkbeard is a deep-water cod relative of the eastern Atlantic with long, forked pelvic fins used to feel for food.

entities.name: Southern blue whiting
entities.fact: The southern blue whiting is a cod relative of sub-Antarctic waters fished off New Zealand, Argentina and the Falklands.

entities.name: Argentine hake
entities.fact: The Argentine hake is the most important fish of Argentina's fisheries, trawled over the Patagonian shelf.

entities.name: Burbot
entities.fact: The burbot is the only member of the cod family that lives in fresh water, a bottom-dwelling, eel-like fish that spawns under the ice in midwinter.

entities.name: Red snapper
entities.fact: The northern red snapper of the Gulf of Mexico can live for over 50 years and is so popular that many cheaper fish are passed off as it in restaurants.
